name: Slime Green
lede: Slime Green is a vivid yellow-green listed by CSS, RAL, Ridgway, the ISCC-NBS and xkcd's crowdsourced survey.

sections.title: A vivid green with six names at once
sections.body:
This exact hue is unusually well attested across systems: Ridgway's 1912 atlas lists it on plate VI as hue 31, RAL lists it as RAL 6018, the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 places it in block 116 and calls it a vivid yellow green, and the crowdsourced xkcd color survey of 2010 names it too [1]. The ISCC-NBS block alone holds at least seven near-duplicate entries, among them Bright Chartreuse, Greenery and Night Green, a reminder that a vivid, saturated hue like this one tends to attract many names rather than one [1].

The books read give no coiner for the specific phrase *slime green*, and its origin is undocumented here [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[sheen-green]], [[yellowish-green]] and [[apple-green]], at 2.8, 4.6 and 6.0 ΔE [1]. It also sits near [[chartreuse]] and [[lime-green]] in our library, two other vivid yellow-greens [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
No painting in our 23,781-painting archive has a color within four units of Slime Green covering even one per cent of its canvas, as photographed [2]. That describes this archive of historical museum paintings, not painting as a whole, and is itself informative: a color this vivid and this yellow-green rarely survived as a natural pigment or dye before synthetic colorants existed [2].

In printed English the phrase *slime green* is essentially absent before 1960, rises through the 1990s, and peaks around 2010, tracking its [2]. use as the name of a specific, brash shade in design and branding rather than any older sense of the words [2].

origin.named_after: undocumented; a modern, brash green name
origin.first_recorded: 1912 (Ridgway, as a swatch); the phrase "slime green" itself rises only after 1960
